summary: Question: how does Winton's founder describe the scientific, data-driven basis of his systematic hedge fund. Method: FT magazine profile and interview (Nov 2016), no data tests. Conclusion: edge comes from many weak signals across markets found by empirical research, with continual replacement as signals decay.

coverage.note: profile intro, Harding's 1994 paper idea; biography otherwise nothing more actionable
nothing actionable: full-page portrait with magazine footer only

research philosophy, weak-signal approach, universe, weather/seasonal/inventory indicators, signal decay, behavioural premise, track record claim, industry size; biography, philanthropy and tax comments skipped as not strategy-relevant

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (reporting Harding)
claims.quote: Harding’s idea was that finance could use science to identify and exploit inefficiencies in the markets.
claims.claim: Interviewer's framing: Harding (1994 Royal Society paper 'Making money from mathematical models') argued finance could use science to find and exploit market inefficiencies; Winton manages $32bn.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: research in the manner of a science experiment – collecting and organising data, making observa- tions and developing hypotheses and then testing these hypotheses against empirical evidence.
claims.claim: Winton runs research like a science experiment: collect and organise data, observe, form hypotheses, test against empirical evidence.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: We don’t make assumptions about how markets should work, rather we use advanced statistical techniques to seek patterns in huge datasets and base all our investment strategies on the analysis of empirical evidence.
claims.claim: Strategies are derived by statistical pattern search in large datasets with no prior assumptions about how markets should work, relying on 'scientific methods' to extract meaning from noisy market data.
claims.exact_rule: data-driven pattern search in huge datasets; every strategy based on empirical evidence, not theory

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: The aim is to exploit a large number of weak predictive signals, he says:
claims.claim: Aim is to exploit a large number of weak predictive signals across many markets rather than a few strong ones.
claims.exact_rule: combine many weak predictive signals across a broad set of markets
claims.indicator: large number of weak predictive signals
claims.testable: partly - signal count and weighting not given

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: We don’t expect to find any strong relationships between data and the price of the market.
claims.claim: Strong relationships are likely already being exploited by others, so edge lies in weak relationships.
claims.conditions: Weak relationships are where the firm has a competitive advantage

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (reporting Harding)
claims.quote: Harding emphasises the breadth and volume of investments involved, covering bonds, currencies, commodities, market indices and individual equi- ties.
claims.claim: Winton trades a broad universe: bonds, currencies, commodities, market indices and individual equities.

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson
claims.quote: Weather strategies are one feature of Winton research, including analysis of cloud cover and soil moisture levels to predict the prices of agricultural commodities.
claims.claim: Winton uses weather data (cloud cover, soil moisture) to predict agricultural commodity prices.
claims.data_needed: weather and soil moisture data; agricultural commodity prices
claims.direction: weather/soil conditions -> agricultural prices (sign not given)
claims.testable: partly - data available, rule not given

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson
claims.quote: Other important indicators, for which maths can uncover value not fully reflected in market prices, include seasonal factors and inventory levels across supply chains.
claims.claim: Other Winton indicators include seasonal factors and inventory levels across supply chains, which they say carry value not fully reflected in prices.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Humans are prone to unpredictable behaviour, to over-reaction or slumbering inaction, to mania and panic.
claims.claim: Winton exploits departures from efficient markets because humans over-react, under-react (slumbering inaction) and swing into mania and panic; economics is a social, not physical, science.
claims.conditions: Efficient market theory said by Harding to still dominate despite evidence against it

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (reporting Harding)
claims.quote: predictive tools lose their power as markets change; new ones are always needed.
claims.claim: Predictive signals decay as markets change, so research is a never-ending process of finding new ones.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: “We have 450 people in the company, of whom 250 are involved in research, data collection or technology,”
claims.claim: Winton has 450 staff, 250 of them in research, data collection or technology, i.e. heavy investment in continual signal discovery.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: we have used techniques that would be described as machine learning for at least 30 years.”
claims.claim: Harding says Winton has used techniques that count as machine learning for at least 30 years (describes the upsurge in AI excitement as not new).

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson
claims.quote: Those clients have seen a compound annual growth rate of 12.8 per cent, net of fees.
claims.claim: Reported client compound annual growth rate 12.8% net of fees (period and fund not specified in the article).
claims.reported_result: 12.8% CAGR net of fees; sample period, product and share class not stated
claims.conditions: Unverified claim in a magazine interview; seems to cover clients since inception

claims.speaker: Clive Cookson (reporting Harding)
claims.quote: Harding admits to using science and mathemat- ics as a marketing tool to sell Winton to institu- tional clients
claims.claim: Harding concedes science is partly a marketing tool for institutional clients ('there is certainly an element of truth in that') but insists science controls the strategy.

claims.speaker: Unnamed quantitative fund manager
claims.quote: I would estimate that systematic or mathe- matical funds amount to 15 per cent of assets in the hedge fund industry – somewhere between $330bn and $450bn altogether.
claims.claim: Anonymous quant manager estimates systematic funds at about 15% of hedge fund assets ($330-450bn); article also cites Renaissance Technologies at $65bn.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: “It treats economics like a physical science when, in fact, it is a human or social science.
claims.claim: Harding argues efficient market theory wrongly treats economics as a physical science, which is why patterns from human behaviour persist.

claims.speaker: David Harding (1994 paper)
claims.quote: all the intellectual purity of selling vegetables
claims.claim: Harding contrasts his approach with conventional bank and broker revenue sources (fees, selling marked-up complex derivatives, arbitrage), which he says have 'all the intellectual purity of selling vegetables'.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Essentially, he says, quantitative investing, self- driving cars and speech recognition are all applica- tions of “information engineering”.
claims.claim: Harding sees quantitative investing as 'information engineering', the same family as speech recognition, with much scope for improvement.
